title: Describe thread-safety in StringBuffer and how it compares to String and StringBuilder.
shortTitle: How is StringBuffer thread-safe compared to String and StringBuilder?

s1_definition.profdef: `StringBuffer` is thread-safe because every one of its mutating and reading methods is synchronized on the StringBuffer instance, so concurrent calls from multiple threads are serialized and the internal buffer cannot be corrupted. `String` is thread-safe by a completely different mechanism: it is immutable, so there is no mutable state to protect and no synchronization is needed at all. `StringBuilder` is not thread-safe; it has the same API as StringBuffer but without synchronization, so concurrent mutation can corrupt it, and it is intended for single-threaded use where its lack of locking makes it faster. So all three can be used safely with threads, but String achieves safety through immutability, StringBuffer through locking, and StringBuilder only when confined to one thread.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, picture three ways to keep a record safe when many clerks are around. A String is like a printed certificate nobody can edit, so it is automatically safe no matter how many clerks hold it. A StringBuffer is like a shared logbook with a single pen chained to it, so only one clerk can write at a time; it is safe because of the enforced turn-taking. A StringBuilder is like an open notepad with no pen rule, perfectly fine for one clerk working alone and very quick, but if several clerks scribble at once the page becomes an unreadable mess. The bank picks the method based on whether the record changes and whether many clerks share it.
s1_definition.oneliner: String is thread-safe by immutability, StringBuffer by synchronization, and StringBuilder is unsynchronized and safe only within a single thread.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `StringBuffer` is thread-safe because every one of its mutating and reading methods is synchronized on the StringBuffer instance, so concurrent calls from multiple threads are serialized and the internal buffer cannot be corrupted. `String` is thread-safe by a completely different mechanism: it is immutable, so there is no mutable state to protect and no synchronization is needed at all. `StringBuilder` is not thread-safe; it has the same API as StringBuffer but without synchronization, so concurrent mutation can corrupt it, and it is intended for single-threaded use where its lack of locking makes it faster. So all three can be used safely with threads, but String achieves safety through immutability, StringBuffer through locking, and StringBuilder only when confined to one thread.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, picture three ways to keep a record safe when many clerks are around. A String is like a printed certificate nobody can edit, so it is automatically safe no matter how many clerks hold it. A StringBuffer is like a shared logbook with a single pen chained to it, so only one clerk can write at a time; it is safe because of the enforced turn-taking. A StringBuilder is like an open notepad with no pen rule, perfectly fine for one clerk working alone and very quick, but if several clerks scribble at once the page becomes an unreadable mess. The bank picks the method based on whether the record changes and whether many clerks share it.

**One line to remember:** String is thread-safe by immutability, StringBuffer by synchronization, and StringBuilder is unsynchronized and safe only within a single thread.

sections.s2_technical:
StringBuffer achieves thread-safety by synchronization. Each public method such as append, insert, delete, and even length and toString is marked synchronized, which means a thread must acquire the buffer's intrinsic lock before executing the method. This serializes access, so two threads cannot interleave their modifications and corrupt the shared char array or the count field. The synchronization also provides memory visibility, so one thread's changes are visible to another after the lock is released and reacquired.

String achieves thread-safety without any locking, purely through immutability. Because a String's contents are set once and can never change, multiple threads can read the same String simultaneously with zero coordination. There is no write, so there is no race. The Java Memory Model's final-field guarantee ensures the constructed value is visible to all threads. This is the cheapest possible form of thread-safety.

StringBuilder deliberately omits synchronization. Its methods modify the shared buffer without any lock, so if two threads append concurrently, their read-modify-write sequences on the count and the array can interleave, producing corrupted output, lost characters, or even exceptions like ArrayIndexOutOfBounds. StringBuilder is therefore safe only when a single thread uses it, or when each thread has its own instance. In exchange it avoids all locking overhead, which is why it is faster than StringBuffer for the common single-threaded case.

A senior nuance is that StringBuffer's method-level synchronization makes each individual call atomic but does not make a sequence of calls atomic. If a thread does append then checks length then appends again, another thread can interleave between those calls, so compound invariants still need external synchronization. Because of this limited guarantee and the ubiquity of single-threaded string building, modern practice is to use StringBuilder almost everywhere and reserve StringBuffer for the rare case of a genuinely shared mutable buffer. Another nuance is that for high-concurrency logging or aggregation, a common pattern is thread-local StringBuilders combined at the end, which avoids lock contention entirely and outperforms a shared StringBuffer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank writes a shared transaction audit trail from many worker threads at once and must guarantee no entry is lost or garbled. This is exactly where StringBuffer's synchronization provides safety.

Problem 2 — A developer tried the same shared-buffer pattern with a StringBuilder and the audit trail came out corrupted with lost and interleaved characters. This is exactly StringBuilder's lack of thread-safety.

Problem 3 — The immutable account id is read by all threads with no coordination, showing String's immutability-based safety. This is exactly String's thread-safety.

The code runs many threads against both a shared StringBuffer and a shared StringBuilder, and a `ThreadSafetyBufferDemo` main class compares the resulting line counts.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: 6 threads, each recording 500 audit entries, so the expected line count is 3000, written to both a shared StringBuffer and a shared StringBuilder.

Step 1: The account id SAV2001 is an immutable String. Every thread reads it to build its entry text with no coordination, because immutable data cannot be corrupted by concurrent reads.

Step 2: Each thread appends its entry to the shared StringBuffer. Because append is synchronized, each thread must take the buffer's lock, so appends are serialized and no two interleave.

Step 3: The same entry is also appended to the shared StringBuilder, which is not synchronized, so concurrent appends race on the internal count and array.

Step 4: After all threads finish, the StringBuffer contains exactly 3000 intact lines, because synchronization prevented corruption.

Step 5: The StringBuilder usually contains the wrong number of lines, with characters lost or interleaved, because the unsynchronized read-modify-write operations collided.

Step 6: Comparing the two counts shows StringBuffer preserved every entry while StringBuilder corrupted the shared buffer, demonstrating synchronization-based safety versus the unsafe single-threaded-only builder, with String safe throughout by immutability.

```text
INFO: Expected lines = 3000
INFO: StringBuffer (safe) lines  = 3000 (CORRECT)
WARNING: StringBuilder (unsafe) lines = 2731 (likely wrong/corrupted)
```
sections.s5b_flow:

```text
  6 threads × 500 appends

  ─── StringBuffer (synchronized) ───

  w1 ─┼─ append() must take LOCK → serialized → buffer intact
  ... │
  w5 ─┘
        ▼ 3000 lines

  ─── StringBuilder (no lock) ───
  w0 ─┐
  w1 ─┼─ append() races on count/array → interleave → corruption

  w5 ─┘
        ▼ 2731 lines (lost/garbled)
```

```text
  ┌────────────┐  N threads ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Txn workers│──────────→ │ SafeAudit         │  StringBuffer (synchronized)
  │ (×6)       │            │ shared buffer     │  → no corruption
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Thread-Safety Mechanisms ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Type          safety mechanism      cost        │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ String        immutability          none (free) │
  │ StringBuffer  synchronized methods  lock per call│
  │ StringBuilder none (single-thread)  fastest, racy if shared │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  StringBuffer.append (conceptual):
    synchronized(this) { ensureCapacity; copy chars; count += n; }
    → each call atomic ; sequence of calls NOT atomic

  Rules:
   read-only shared text         → String (immutable)
   shared mutable buffer, threads→ StringBuffer (or external lock)
   single-thread building        → StringBuilder (fast)
   high-concurrency aggregation  → thread-local StringBuilder + merge
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
StringBuffer is thread-safe because every one of its methods is synchronized on the buffer instance. A thread must acquire the buffer's intrinsic lock before running a method, which serializes concurrent access so that two threads cannot interleave their modifications and corrupt the internal character array or the length count. The lock also provides memory visibility, so one thread's changes are seen by another after the lock is released and reacquired.

It is worth contrasting the three types, because they achieve safety very differently. String is thread-safe with no locking at all, purely through immutability. Since a String's contents are fixed at construction and can never change, any number of threads can read the same String at once with zero coordination, because there is no write and therefore no race. That is the cheapest possible thread-safety. StringBuilder, on the other hand, is deliberately not synchronized. It has the same API as StringBuffer but without locks, so if two threads append to it concurrently, their read-modify-write sequences on the count and array interleave, producing lost characters, garbled output, or even an exception. StringBuilder is safe only when confined to a single thread or when each thread has its own instance, and in return it avoids all locking overhead, which makes it faster for the common single-threaded case.

I demonstrated this with a concurrent audit trail. Six threads appended to a shared StringBuffer and a shared StringBuilder at the same time. The StringBuffer ended with exactly the expected number of lines because synchronization kept every append intact, while the StringBuilder lost and garbled entries because its appends raced.

The senior nuance I always add is that StringBuffer only makes each single method call atomic, not a sequence of calls, so if I need a compound operation to stay consistent I still need external synchronization. Because of that limited guarantee, and because most string building is single-threaded, modern practice is to use StringBuilder almost everywhere, String for fixed shared text, and StringBuffer only for a genuinely shared mutable buffer. And for high-concurrency aggregation in our banking services, I usually prefer giving each thread its own StringBuilder and merging the results at the end, which eliminates lock contention entirely and outperforms a single shared StringBuffer.

---

keyPoints: StringBuffer: every method is synchronized — one thread at a time
StringBuilder: no synchronization — faster but NOT safe for concurrent access
String: inherently thread-safe because it is immutable
In practice, StringBuilder is preferred — thread safety rarely needed for building strings
